title: Depth-First Search
summary: Follow one path as far as it goes, then back up and try the next — the natural shape for exploring everything, detecting cycles, and ordering dependencies.

analogy.beginner: Exploring a cave with a ball of string. You take the first tunnel and keep going until it dead-ends. Then you follow the string back to the last junction and take the next tunnel. You will see the entire cave — just not in any order related to distance from the entrance. The string is the call stack, and reeling it back in is what 'backtracking' means.
analogy.interview: Traversal that fully explores each branch before backtracking, implemented by recursion (implicit stack) or an explicit stack. O(V + E) with an adjacency list. It gives no shortest-path guarantee, but its recursion structure makes it the natural fit for connectivity, cycle detection, topological sorting and any problem where you need results computed bottom-up from children.

intuition:
BFS asks 'what is nearby?'. DFS asks 'where does this lead?'.

The code is almost embarrassingly short — visit, mark, recurse into each unvisited neighbour — but the shape does three distinct jobs:

**Exhaustive exploration.** Anything reachable will be reached. Counting connected components, flood fill, 'how many islands' — all of this is 'start a DFS from each unvisited node and see how many times you have to start'.

**Bottom-up computation.** Because a recursive call returns *after* the subtree is finished, DFS is how you compute things that depend on your children: subtree sizes, tree height, whether a subtree is balanced. BFS cannot do this naturally.

**Ordering and cycles.** Recording nodes as you *finish* them (post-order) and reversing gives a topological order. Tracking which nodes are on the *current* path detects cycles in a directed graph. Both fall out of the stack discipline, and both are commonly asked.

The one thing to be careful about is the distinction between the two 'visited' concepts in directed graphs: `visited` (ever seen — never process twice) and `onPath`/`inStack` (currently on the recursion path — a repeat here is a cycle). Conflating them is the classic bug.

problemFirst.motivatingProblem: You have course prerequisites: to take B you must first take A. Can every course be completed, or is there a circular dependency?

bruteForce.idea: For each course, follow its prerequisite chains and see whether you ever come back to where you started.

bruteForce.whySlow: Every course re-explores the graph from scratch, with no memory carried between runs. Whole subgraphs already proven acyclic are re-walked V times.

problemFirst.observation: A cycle exists exactly when, during a single depth-first walk, we reach a node that is already on the path we are currently standing on. Nodes we finished exploring earlier are settled — they can never be part of a new cycle.
problemFirst.leap: One DFS with two marks: `visited` (settled, never look again) and `onPath` (on the current recursion stack — meeting one of these is a cycle). One O(V + E) pass answers it for the whole graph.

howItWorks: **Recursive form** — `visit(node)`: if visited, return; mark visited; process; recurse into each neighbour. This is the form to write unless the depth could be enormous.

**Iterative form** — push the start on a stack; pop, mark, push unvisited neighbours. Necessary when depth might overflow the call stack. Note the visit order differs from the recursive version (neighbours come off in reverse).

**Pre-order vs post-order** — work done *before* recursing flows top-down (passing context to children); work done *after* flows bottom-up (aggregating results from children). Choosing the side is usually the whole design.
**Connected components** — loop over all vertices; each unvisited one starts a new DFS, and the number of starts is the number of components.
**Cycle detection, directed** — keep `visited` and `onPath`; hitting an `onPath` node is a back edge, i.e. a cycle. Clear `onPath` when the call returns.
**Cycle detection, undirected** — a cycle is any visited neighbour that is not the node you just came from; pass the parent down.
**Topological sort** — append each node to a list when its DFS call *finishes*, then reverse. Valid only on a DAG.

complexity.time: O(V + E) — O(rows × cols) on a grid
complexity.space: O(V) for visited, plus O(h) for the recursion stack where h is the longest path
complexity.why: Each vertex is processed once and each edge examined once, exactly as in BFS. The difference is the auxiliary memory profile: DFS holds one root-to-leaf path on the stack, so it is O(log n) on a balanced tree but O(n) on a skewed one or a long chain — and that O(n) is *call stack*, which is far more limited than heap. A DFS a million nodes deep will throw StackOverflowError while the equivalent BFS merely uses a large queue. That is the practical reason to know the iterative form.

commonMistakes.mistake: Conflating `visited` with `onPath` in directed cycle detection
commonMistakes.fix: Two different marks. `visited` prevents rework; `onPath` (cleared when the call returns) is what actually detects the cycle.

commonMistakes.mistake: Marking visited after recursing instead of before
commonMistakes.fix: In a cyclic graph you recurse forever. Mark on entry.
A 100,000-node chain exceeds the default JVM stack. Use the iterative form, or raise `-Xss` deliberately.

commonMistakes.mistake: Undirected cycle detection flagging the edge you just came along
commonMistakes.fix: Every undirected edge looks like a 2-cycle. Pass the parent and skip it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using DFS for a shortest-path question
commonMistakes.fix: DFS finds *a* path, not the shortest. Use BFS.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to clear state on the way out in backtracking problems
commonMistakes.fix: Whatever you add before recursing must be removed after. See the Backtracking lesson.

realWorldUses: Build systems and package managers topologically sort dependency graphs; a cycle is the 'circular dependency' error you have seen.
Spring's application context detects circular bean dependencies with exactly this algorithm.
Deadlock detection: a cycle in the wait-for graph.
Compilers walk ASTs depth-first for type checking and code generation; linters compute scope information bottom-up.
Filesystem traversal (`find`, `du`), garbage-collection mark phases, and maze generation.
interviewNotes: 'BFS or DFS?' — answer with the guarantee you need. Shortest path ⇒ BFS. Everything reachable, results from children, ordering, cycles ⇒ DFS.
For tree questions, ask yourself: what do I need from my children, and what do I return to my parent? That converts almost any tree problem into a post-order DFS.
Course Schedule (I and II) is the standard topological-sort pair. Knowing both the DFS colouring and Kahn's in-degree version is worth the extra twenty minutes.

quiz.question: Which data structure does recursive DFS implicitly use?
quiz.explanation: Each recursive call pushes a frame; returning pops it. Converting DFS to an iterative algorithm just means managing that stack yourself with a Deque.

quiz.question: In directed cycle detection, why are two separate marks needed?
options: `visited` stops rework on settled nodes; `onPath` identifies a back edge to a node on the current recursion path, which is what a cycle is
One is for nodes, one for edges
Only one mark is actually needed
quiz.explanation: Revisiting a node that was fully explored earlier is harmless — it is a cross edge. Revisiting a node still on the current path means you have walked in a circle.

quiz.question: 'Count the number of islands in a grid of land and water.' Which approach?
options: DFS/BFS flood fill from each unvisited land cell, counting how many times you must start
quiz.explanation: Each fresh start marks a new connected component, and the flood fill absorbs all of it so it is never counted twice. DFS and BFS both work; DFS is shorter to write.

quiz.question: How do you produce a topological order with DFS?
options: Record nodes when you first visit them
Record each node when its DFS call *finishes*, then reverse the list
Use a queue instead of recursion
quiz.explanation: A node finishes only after everything it depends on has finished, so finish order is reverse topological order. Pushing onto a stack as you finish yields the correct order directly.
